runs.goal: find out how the most recent Starship booster catch compares to the first booster catch
runs.detail:
I couldn't save the Notion page: Notion is switched off here and both attempts failed, which also blocked the normal finish. Here is the comparison instead.

**The two catches**
- **First:** Flight 5, October 13, 2024, Booster 12.
- **Most recent:** Flight 8, March 6, 2025, Booster 15.
- Booster 14 on Flight 7 was the only other one, so the record is three catches in total.

**How they compare**
- **Margin:** Flight 5 worked on the first try but only just. SpaceX engineers later said a misconfigured spin-gas setting left the booster one second from an automatic abort. A chine cover also came off on the way down.
- **Engines:** Flight 8 succeeded despite engine trouble. Only 11 of 13 engines lit for the boostback burn, and a fan wiki reports 12 of 13 for the landing burn.
- **Approach:** Booster 15 came in to the tower with less sideways motion than earlier catches.
- **After the catch:** Booster 12 had warped outer engine nozzles and was retired. Two of the three caught boosters later flew again.
- **Rest of the flight:** on Flight 8 the upper stage, Ship 34, was lost, so the booster catch was that mission's main success.

**Since then**
No booster has been caught since Flight 8. On Flight 15 (November 13, 2026), Booster 22 called off its own catch after a low-fuel alarm cut the boostback burn short, and it was lost in the Gulf. A day later the same flight made the first-ever tower catch of the upper stage, Ship 42.

Sources: NASASpaceFlight (Flight 5 and Flight 8 reports), Space.com, Spaceflight Now, SpaceQ, Wikipedia's list of Super Heavy boosters, and the Starship fan wiki.

sections.heading: The two catches at a glance
points: First catch: Flight 5, October 13, 2024, Booster 12 (Block 1), caught at Starbase about six to seven minutes after a 7:25 am Central liftoff.
Most recent catch: Flight 8, March 6, 2025, Booster 15, also caught at Starbase's first pad.
Between them sits one more success (Booster 14 on Flight 7), so the record is three catches: Flights 5, 7 and 8.
No booster has been caught since Flight 8. The Flight 15 attempt on November 13, 2026 was called off and Booster 22 was lost in the Gulf.

sections.heading: First catch: Flight 5, Booster 12
points: It worked on the very first attempt, with SpaceX manually giving the go for the catch after checking booster and tower.
The margin was thin: engineers later said a misconfigured spin-gas setting left the booster one second from triggering an abort that would have crashed it beside the tower.
A cover over one of the booster's chines came off during descent, another issue that could have scuttled the catch.
Post-catch damage included warped outer engine nozzles, described by Musk as easy to address. Booster 12 was retired and never flew again.

sections.heading: Most recent catch: Flight 8, Booster 15
points: Engine trouble did not stop it: only 11 of 13 engines lit for the boostback burn, and 12 of 13 reportedly relit for the landing burn.
The approach profile changed: Booster 15 came in to the tower with less sideways motion than earlier catches.
Observers described the catch as looking unusually hard, yet it held.
The ship half of the flight failed. Ship 34 lost several engines and attitude control and was destroyed, so the booster catch was the mission's main success.

sections.heading: What changed between them
points: Confidence: Flight 5 proved the idea could work at all; by Flight 8 the catch had succeeded three times in four attempts (Flight 6 diverted to the sea).
Robustness: Flight 5 succeeded with a nearly tripped abort; Flight 8 succeeded despite engines failing to relight.
Reuse: the first caught booster was retired, while two of the three caught boosters went on to fly again.
Flight 8's approach was refined to reduce horizontal movement near the tower.

sections.heading: Since the last catch
points: Roughly 20 months and several flights have passed without another booster catch.
On Flight 15 (November 13, 2026), the new Version 3 Booster 22 ended its boostback burn early after a low-fuel-mass alarm, diverted offshore on its own, and exploded at the water.
A day later the same flight delivered the first ever tower catch of a Starship upper stage, Ship 42, returning from orbit.
A Version 3 Super Heavy has not yet been caught.

runs.goal: find out how the most recent Starship booster catch compares to the first booster catch
runs.detail: The most recent booster catch is still Flight 8 in March 2025. Compared with the first catch in October 2024, it came in with less sideways motion, keeping exhaust off the tower, and worked despite two engines not lighting. The latest attempt, this November, was called off.

sections.heading: First catch: Flight 5, October 13, 2024
points: Booster 12 flew with Ship 30 and was caught by the Starbase launch tower arms on the very first attempt.
Liftoff was at 7:25 am CDT and the booster was in the arms at about 7:32 am, roughly seven minutes later.
The catch was not automatic: the booster and tower had to pass health checks, and a go command was needed before the booster could head back to the tower.
It proved the idea worked: a tower can catch a returning Super Heavy instead of the booster needing landing legs.

sections.heading: Most recent catch: Flight 8, March 2025
points: Booster 15 was caught by the tower, making it the third successful Super Heavy catch (Booster 14 on Flight 7 was the second).
Only 11 of the 13 engines lit for the boostback burn, yet the booster still made it back and was caught.
The approach was refined: Booster 15 came in with less sideways motion than earlier catches, so engine exhaust stayed off the launch mount and the tower.
The three centre engines kept burning to steer the booster into the arms.
The upper stage, Ship 34, was lost on the same flight after several engines shut down early.

sections.heading: How the two compare
points: Same method and same site: tower arms at Starbase, a booster of the older design each time.
Flight 5 was a proof of concept; Flight 8 was a cleaner, gentler approach designed to spare the pad from exhaust damage.
Flight 8 showed more margin, succeeding despite two engines failing to light on the boostback burn.
Caught boosters became reusable hardware: Booster 14 was the first Super Heavy to fly again (Flight 9), and Booster 15 flew again on Flight 11, where it was expended.

sections.heading: What has happened since
points: No booster has been caught since March 2025.
On Flight 15 (November 13, 2026) SpaceX tried the first catch of the larger Version 3 booster, called it off, and sent the booster to a splashdown in the Gulf. The cause was not yet known.
The next day the tower caught the upper stage, Ship 42, after an orbital flight, the first ever ship catch.
Total booster catches stand at three: Flights 5, 7 and 8.

runs.goal: find out what the James Webb Space Telescope's mirror is made of and why
runs.detail: Webb's mirror is made of beryllium with a very thin coating of gold. Beryllium is light, stiff, and holds its shape in extreme cold, while gold reflects infrared light, which Webb is built to see, extremely well. The notes page could not be saved because Notion was unavailable.

sections.heading: The body: beryllium
points: All 18 hexagonal segments of the primary mirror, plus the secondary mirror, are machined from beryllium, a light metal.
Low weight: one segment is about 20 kg on its own. The whole primary mirror is about 705 kg, lighter than Hubble's 825 kg glass mirror despite having more than five times the area.
Stiffness: beryllium is very rigid, so thin segments keep their precise curve through launch and in use.
Cold stability: Webb works at cryogenic temperatures, and beryllium barely expands or shrinks as temperature changes, so the shape stays true in deep cold.
The metal was mined in Utah and purified in Ohio.

sections.heading: The surface: gold
points: Bare beryllium is not a good enough reflector for Webb's needs, so each polished segment gets a gold film.
Gold is an excellent reflector of infrared light, which is the light Webb is built to observe (roughly 600 to 28,500 nanometres).
Gold is also chemically unreactive, so it does not tarnish easily.

The film is only about 100 to 120 nanometres thick, around 200 times thinner than a human hair. It had to cover the surface fully yet stay thin enough not to distort the mirror as temperatures change.
It was applied by vacuum vapour deposition, and a thin glass layer on top protects the soft gold.

sections.heading: Compared with Hubble
points: Webb: segmented beryllium coated with gold, tuned for infrared.
Hubble: a single glass mirror coated with aluminium and magnesium fluoride, tuned mainly for visible and ultraviolet light.

runs.goal: find out what the James Webb Space Telescope's mirror is made of and why
runs.detail: Webb's mirror is eighteen beryllium segments with a very thin gold coating. Beryllium is strong, light, and holds its shape in extreme cold. The gold is there because it reflects infrared light, which is what Webb mainly sees, and it resists tarnishing.

sections.heading: What the mirror is made of
points: The main mirror is 18 hexagonal segments that together span about 6.5 meters (21 feet).
Each segment's body is beryllium, a light metal. One segment is roughly the size of a coffee table and weighs about 20 kilograms.
On top of the polished beryllium sits a gold film about 120 nanometers thick, around 200 times thinner than a human hair.
A thin glass layer covers the gold to protect it.
The secondary and other mirrors use the same beryllium-plus-gold recipe.

sections.heading: Why beryllium
points: Strength with low weight: launch mass is limited, and a 6.5 meter mirror has to be stiff without being heavy.
Stable shape in extreme cold: Webb runs at cryogenic temperatures, and beryllium keeps its figure there, so the image stays sharp.
An expert panel recommended beryllium for these reasons, and Northrop Grumman and NASA Goddard adopted the choice.

sections.heading: Why gold
points: Webb observes mainly in infrared, about 600 to 28,500 nanometers, and gold is an excellent infrared reflector, so more of the faint light reaches the instruments.
Gold barely reacts chemically, so the surface resists tarnishing.
The film had to fully cover the surface yet stay thin enough not to distort the mirror as temperatures change.

sections.heading: How it was made
points: The beryllium came from a mine in Utah and was purified in Ohio.
Segments were shaped, polished, and corrected for how they deform in the cold before coating.
Quantum Coating Inc. applied the gold by vacuum vapor deposition: vaporized gold settles on the optical surface.
The mirror is wider than any rocket fairing, so its two sides folded for launch, and motors behind each segment let the team focus it in space.
